content.summary: Read a city council discussion about public transport, electric vehicles, and traffic. You will identify the main arguments, find supporting details, and notice how conditional sentences help people discuss past decisions and possible changes.

contextWarmup.prompt: A city has limited money for transport. Which change would you support first?
options: More frequent buses and trains
More public electric-car chargers
A larger road for private cars
contextWarmup.explanation: There is no single correct policy for every city. More frequent public transport can help many people travel without using a private car, so it is a strong option to discuss.

rules: Use if + past perfect and would have + past participle to imagine a different past and its past result.
Use if + past perfect and would + base verb to connect a different past with a result in the present.
Use if + past simple and would + base verb to suggest a possible change in the present or future.

commonTrap.explanation: Do not use would in the if-clause in these conditional patterns. Put would in the result clause.

commonTrap.correct: If the city built more bus lanes, traffic would improve.

content.passageTitle: Two Ways to Make City Travel Better
paragraphs: At a recent meeting, Brookford City Council discussed how to improve urban mobility. Traffic is slow in the centre, and many residents drive to work because buses are crowded. The council has money for one major transport project this year. Some members want to improve public transport, while others support electric vehicles.

Councillor Maya Reed argued for more frequent buses and lower fares. She said that if the council subsidised tickets, more commuters would leave their cars at home. A transport report also showed that bus use had fallen because services stopped early in the evening. If the city had kept buses running later, more residents would use them today.

Councillor Ben Hall supported electric vehicles. They do not produce direct carbon emissions while driving, but they are not a complete answer to congestion. Many people cannot afford an electric car, and the city has too few charging points. Hall said that if the council had built more charging infrastructure earlier, more drivers would own electric vehicles now.

Residents asked the council to consider both plans. The report recommended reliable public transport first, together with new charging points over time. It explained that electric cars can reduce pollution, but they still use road space. If Brookford improved buses and trains, fewer people might need a car for every trip. The council will compare the costs before making its decision.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Debating Urban Transport Policies

content.summary: Learn how to construct formal arguments about urban mobility using advanced conditional structures. Master the Third Conditional to critique past planning decisions, the Mixed Conditional to link past policies to present conditions, and the Second Conditional to suggest realistic alternatives.

blueprintItems.title: Third Conditional: Critiquing Past Decisions
blueprintItems.formula: If + Past Perfect (had + V3), Subject + would have + Past Participle (V3)
blueprintItems.example: If the city council had funded the tram network in 2012, traffic congestion would have decreased much earlier.

blueprintItems.title: Mixed Conditional: Past Choice with Present Impact
blueprintItems.formula: If + Past Perfect (had + V3), Subject + would + Base Verb
blueprintItems.example: If urban planners had prioritized bicycle lanes ten years ago, our streets would be safer today.

blueprintItems.title: Second Conditional: Hypothetical Policy Alternatives
blueprintItems.formula: If + Past Simple, Subject + would + Base Verb
blueprintItems.example: If the government subsidized electric buses, commuters would choose public transit more often.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place a comma after the conditional clause when it begins the sentence. Do not use a comma if the main clause comes first.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If electric cars were cheaper more families would buy them.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If electric cars were cheaper, more families would buy them.
mechanicsRules.why: The comma signals to the reader that the introductory condition has finished and the main consequence is starting.

mechanicsRules.rule: Never write 'would of' instead of 'would have'. In formal writing, avoid contractions like 'would've' and 'hadn't'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The city would of reduced air pollution if it hadn't cancelled the metro project.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The city would have reduced air pollution if it had not cancelled the metro project.
mechanicsRules.why: Using 'would of' is a grammatical error caused by how spoken English sounds. Full modal forms are expected in formal policy essays.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize official public transport authorities and government bodies, but keep general transport terms in lowercase.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The ministry of transport should expand the Electric Bus network in Jakarta.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The Ministry of Transport should expand the electric bus network in Jakarta.
mechanicsRules.why: Specific administrative institutions are proper nouns, whereas generic vehicle types and transit modes are common nouns.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Transform this real situation into a Second Conditional sentence starting with 'If':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Electric cars are expensive, so many commuters do not buy them.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'If electric cars were...' or 'If electric cars were not...'
targetAnswers: If electric cars were cheaper, many commuters would buy them.
If electric cars were not so expensive, many commuters would buy them.
If electric cars were less expensive, many commuters would buy them.
practicumQuestions.explanation: To imagine a hypothetical change in the present, use the Second Conditional: 'If + Past Simple, would + base verb'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Transform this past failure into a Third Conditional critique:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The government did not invest in electric buses in 2019, so emissions did not fall.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'If the government had invested...'
targetAnswers: If the government had invested in electric buses in 2019, emissions would have fallen.

practicumQuestions.explanation: A Third Conditional reflects on a past event: 'If + had + V3, would have + V3'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the past action and present result into one Mixed Conditional sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The city built a modern metro network in 2015. As a result, traffic congestion is not terrible today.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start your sentence with 'If the city had not built...'
targetAnswers: If the city had not built a modern metro network in 2015, traffic congestion would be terrible today.
If the city had not built a modern metro network in 2015, traffic congestion would be much worse today.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a Mixed Conditional (Past Perfect in the if-clause, would + base verb in the main clause) to show how a past action affects the present.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence by placing the 'if' clause at the end. Remove unnecessary punctuation:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If planners installed rapid charging points downtown, more taxi drivers would adopt electric cars.
practicumQuestions.hint: Place 'More taxi drivers would adopt...' at the beginning without a comma.
targetAnswers: More taxi drivers would adopt electric cars if planners installed rapid charging points downtown.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When the main clause comes first and the 'if' clause follows, do not use a comma between them.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the two grammatical mistakes (informal phrasing error and punctuation) in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The mayor would of reduced road congestion if he had supported public transit.
practicumQuestions.hint: Change 'would of' to the correct modal form and ensure proper phrasing.
targetAnswers: The mayor would have reduced road congestion if he had supported public transit.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Would of' is incorrect; the correct construction is 'would have'. No comma is needed before 'if'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the negative Third Conditional sentence based on the prompt:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Because transport fares rose sharply, passengers stopped using the subway.
practicumQuestions.hint: Write: 'Passengers would not have stopped using the subway if transport fares...'
targetAnswers: Passengers would not have stopped using the subway if transport fares had not risen sharply.
Passengers would not have stopped using the subway if transport fares had not increased sharply.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use negative past perfect 'had not risen' in the condition and negative modal perfect 'would not have stopped' in the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using a Mixed Conditional to describe the present consequence of this past mistake:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The regional council canceled the suburban rail project five years ago. Now, thousands of commuters are stuck in traffic.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with: 'If the regional council had not canceled...'
targetAnswers: If the regional council had not canceled the suburban rail project five years ago, thousands of commuters would not be stuck in traffic now.
If the regional council had not cancelled the suburban rail project five years ago, thousands of commuters would not be stuck in traffic now.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The past condition takes 'had not canceled/cancelled', and the present outcome takes 'would not be stuck'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and comma errors in this policy sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: if the ministry of transport subsidised battery charging stations more drivers would choose evs.
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the government ministry, the start of the sentence, the acronym, and insert a comma.
targetAnswers: If the Ministry of Transport subsidised battery charging stations, more drivers would choose EVs.
If the Ministry of Transport subsidized battery charging stations, more drivers would choose EVs.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Capitalize 'If', 'Ministry of Transport', and 'EVs'. Add a comma after the conditional clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'Unless' instead of 'If':
practicumQuestions.promptText: If the city does not modernize bus routes, air pollution will continue to rise.
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Unless' replaces 'If ... not'. Remember that the verb becomes affirmative: 'Unless the city modernizes...'
targetAnswers: Unless the city modernizes bus routes, air pollution will continue to rise.
Air pollution will continue to rise unless the city modernizes bus routes.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not'. It is followed by an affirmative verb: 'Unless the city modernizes bus routes...'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the policy facts into a single Second Conditional recommendation sentence starting with 'If':
practicumQuestions.promptText: City councils rarely allocate special lanes for electric buses. Therefore, commuters do not travel fast.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'If city councils allocated... commuters would...'
targetAnswers: If city councils allocated special lanes for electric buses, commuters would travel faster.
If city councils allocated special lanes for electric buses, commuters would travel fast.
If city councils provided special lanes for electric buses, commuters would travel faster.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Second Conditional presents a clear policy recommendation: 'If + Past Simple (allocated), Subject + would + base verb (would travel)'.

content.summary: Practise discussing public transport and electric vehicles. Give reasons for your opinions, compare possible solutions, and use conditional sentences to explain what might happen if a city changes its transport policies.
content.audioGuidance: Speak clearly and divide longer ideas into short phrases. Stress important words such as transport, emissions, and congestion. Use a falling tone when you finish a statement. Use a rising tone when you ask a yes-or-no question, and keep your voice calm when you disagree.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.explanation: Make the vowel sounds clear in words such as bus, charge, and train. Do not rush the vowel in longer words such as sustainable.

pillars.name: Word Stress
pillars.explanation: Say transPORT and susTAINable with a clear main stress. This helps listeners understand longer transport words.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress
pillars.explanation: Give more stress to important words: If the city subsidised buses, fewer people would drive. Keep smaller grammar words lighter.

Our senior analyst who joined the firm last January, presented the financial forecast.

Store physical inventory outside the warehouse boundaries.
Follow standard operating procedures without deviation.

David said that he has submitted the report.
David said that he will submit the report.

reading.answer: David said that he had submitted the report.

with

reading.question: What distinction exists between 'economic' and 'economical'?

'Economic' means inexpensive, whereas 'economical' relates to government finance.

'Economical' is only used as a noun, whereas 'economic' is an adverb.
reading.answer: 'Economic' relates to the economy, whereas 'economical' means avoiding waste or saving money.
reading.explanation: 'Economic' refers to national financial systems, while 'economical' refers to frugality or efficiency.

writing.instruction: Transform this real situation into a Second Conditional sentence starting with 'If':
writing.promptText: Electric cars are expensive, so many commuters do not buy them.
writing.hint: Use 'If electric cars were...' or 'If electric cars were not...'
targetAnswers: If electric cars were cheaper, many commuters would buy them.
If electric cars were not so expensive, many commuters would buy them.
If electric cars were less expensive, many commuters would buy them.
writing.explanation: To imagine a hypothetical change in the present, use the Second Conditional: 'If + Past Simple, would + base verb'.

writing.instruction: Transform this past failure into a Third Conditional critique:
writing.promptText: The government did not invest in electric buses in 2019, so emissions did not fall.
writing.hint: Start with 'If the government had invested...'
targetAnswers: If the government had invested in electric buses in 2019, emissions would have fallen.
If the government had invested in electric buses in 2019, emissions would have dropped.
writing.explanation: A Third Conditional reflects on a past event: 'If + had + V3, would have + V3'.

writing.instruction: Combine the past action and present result into one Mixed Conditional sentence:
writing.promptText: The city built a modern metro network in 2015. As a result, traffic congestion is not terrible today.
writing.hint: Start your sentence with 'If the city had not built...'
targetAnswers: If the city had not built a modern metro network in 2015, traffic congestion would be terrible today.
If the city had not built a modern metro network in 2015, traffic congestion would be much worse today.
writing.explanation: Use a Mixed Conditional (Past Perfect in the if-clause, would + base verb in the main clause) to show how a past action affects the present.

writing.instruction: Rewrite the sentence by placing the 'if' clause at the end. Remove unnecessary punctuation:
writing.promptText: If planners installed rapid charging points downtown, more taxi drivers would adopt electric cars.
writing.hint: Place 'More taxi drivers would adopt...' at the beginning without a comma.
targetAnswers: More taxi drivers would adopt electric cars if planners installed rapid charging points downtown.
writing.explanation: When the main clause comes first and the 'if' clause follows, do not use a comma between them.

writing.instruction: Correct the two grammatical mistakes (informal phrasing error and punctuation) in this sentence:
writing.promptText: The mayor would of reduced road congestion if he had supported public transit.
writing.hint: Change 'would of' to the correct modal form and ensure proper phrasing.
targetAnswers: The mayor would have reduced road congestion if he had supported public transit.
writing.explanation: 'Would of' is incorrect; the correct construction is 'would have'. No comma is needed before 'if'.

writing.instruction: Complete the negative Third Conditional sentence based on the prompt:
writing.promptText: Because transport fares rose sharply, passengers stopped using the subway.
writing.hint: Write: 'Passengers would not have stopped using the subway if transport fares...'
targetAnswers: Passengers would not have stopped using the subway if transport fares had not risen sharply.
Passengers would not have stopped using the subway if transport fares had not increased sharply.
writing.explanation: Use negative past perfect 'had not risen' in the condition and negative modal perfect 'would not have stopped' in the main clause.

writing.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using a Mixed Conditional to describe the present consequence of this past mistake:
writing.promptText: The regional council canceled the suburban rail project five years ago. Now, thousands of commuters are stuck in traffic.
writing.hint: Start with: 'If the regional council had not canceled...'
targetAnswers: If the regional council had not canceled the suburban rail project five years ago, thousands of commuters would not be stuck in traffic now.
If the regional council had not cancelled the suburban rail project five years ago, thousands of commuters would not be stuck in traffic now.
writing.explanation: The past condition takes 'had not canceled/cancelled', and the present outcome takes 'would not be stuck'.

writing.instruction: Correct the capitalization and comma errors in this policy sentence:
writing.promptText: if the ministry of transport subsidised battery charging stations more drivers would choose evs.
writing.hint: Capitalize the government ministry, the start of the sentence, the acronym, and insert a comma.
targetAnswers: If the Ministry of Transport subsidised battery charging stations, more drivers would choose EVs.
If the Ministry of Transport subsidized battery charging stations, more drivers would choose EVs.
writing.explanation: Capitalize 'If', 'Ministry of Transport', and 'EVs'. Add a comma after the conditional clause.

writing.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'Unless' instead of 'If':

writing.hint: 'Unless' replaces 'If ... not'. Remember that the verb becomes affirmative: 'Unless the city modernizes...'
targetAnswers: Unless the city modernizes bus routes, air pollution will continue to rise.
Air pollution will continue to rise unless the city modernizes bus routes.
writing.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not'. It is followed by an affirmative verb: 'Unless the city modernizes bus routes...'.

writing.instruction: Combine the policy facts into a single Second Conditional recommendation sentence starting with 'If':

If city councils allocated special lanes for electric buses, commuters would travel fast.
If city councils provided special lanes for electric buses, commuters would travel faster.
writing.explanation: Second Conditional presents a clear policy recommendation: 'If + Past Simple (allocated), Subject + would + base verb (would travel)'.
